text: Nineteen forty five. An engineer is standing next to a radar machine. Then he notices something strange. The chocolate bar in his pocket has melted. <#0.4#> That melted chocolate led to something in almost every kitchen. So how does a box with no fire cook your food? <#0.5#> The engineer was Percy Spencer. He left school at twelve to work in a mill, and taught himself science from books. <#0.4#> During the war, he built magnetrons. That's the part of a radar that sends out invisible waves to spot enemy planes. <#0.4#> After the chocolate, he got curious. He held some corn kernels near the machine. They popped into popcorn. <#0.5#> His company patented the idea. Their first oven, in nineteen forty seven, was taller than a person, and ended up in restaurants and on ships. <#0.4#> So what's the trick? Those invisible waves are like radio waves, only much shorter. We call them microwaves. <#0.5#> Food is full of water. And each tiny water molecule has a plus end and a minus end. <#0.4#> The waves keep flipping those ends back and forth, billions of times every second. All that jiggling makes heat. <#0.5#> Here's a surprise. A microwave doesn't cook from the inside out. The waves only reach a few centimetres in. The rest heats up from the outside, like normal. <#0.5#> Remember the chocolate? Try this with a grown-up. Take out the turntable, and heat a chocolate bar for about twenty seconds. <#0.4#> It melts in spots, where the waves are strongest. Measure the gap between them, do one simple sum, and you get the speed of light. <#0.5#> Today, in the US, ninety six in every hundred homes have a microwave. It all started with one melted chocolate bar. What would you have tested first?
